```{python}
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

growth = pd.read_csv("data/derived/decade_growth.csv")
slopes = pd.read_csv("data/derived/convergence_slopes.csv")

DECADES = list(slopes["decade"])
CONTINENTS = ["Africa", "Asia", "Europe", "North America", "South America", "Oceania"]
COLORS = {"Africa": "#D55E00", "Asia": "#0072B2", "Europe": "#009E73",
          "North America": "#CC79A7", "South America": "#E69F00", "Oceania": "#56B4E9"}

def quartile_growth(decade):
    g = growth[growth["decade"] == decade]
    q = pd.qcut(g["gdp_pc_start"], 4, labels=False)
    return g.loc[q == 0, "growth"].mean(), g.loc[q == 3, "growth"].mean()

s = slopes.set_index("decade")

afr80 = growth[(growth["decade"] == "1980s") & (growth["continent"] == "Africa")]
afr80_n, afr80_shrank = len(afr80), int((afr80["growth"] < 0).sum())
poor60, rich60 = quartile_growth("1960s")
poor00, rich00 = quartile_growth("2000s")
```

Textbook growth theory makes a simple prediction: poor countries should grow faster than
rich ones, because capital is scarce where they are and technology can be borrowed rather
than invented. If that holds, the gap between rich and poor countries shrinks over time,
which economists call convergence.

**The question: in which decades did poor countries actually grow faster than rich ones,
and does the answer change if we count people instead of countries?**

## The data

Penn World Table 11.0 covers 185 economies from 1950 to 2023. For each decade since 1960,
I take every country with at least a million people and compute two things. Income at the
start of the decade uses PWT's expenditure-side GDP at purchasing-power parity, divided by
population, which is built to compare living standards *across* countries. Growth over the
decade uses national-accounts GDP per person, which is built to compare a country with
*itself* over time, expressed as an average annual rate. The 2010s stop in 2019, before the
pandemic. Using two different series also keeps any error in the income level from
mechanically showing up in the growth rate.

## Sixty years in one chart

Each bubble is a country, sized by population. Drag the slider or press play to move
through the decades; hover over a bubble to see which country it is; click a continent in
the legend to hide or isolate it. The dashed line is the fitted relationship for that
decade, with every country counting once.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Income at the start of each decade against average annual growth of GDP per person during it. Bubble size is population. Source: Penn World Table 11.0."

max_pop = growth["pop_start"].max()
sizeref = 2 * max_pop / 55 ** 2

def label(decade):
    return (f"<b>{decade}</b>: slope {s.loc[decade, 'slope']:+.2f} "
            f"({'poorer countries grew faster' if s.loc[decade, 'slope'] < -0.3 else 'richer countries grew faster' if s.loc[decade, 'slope'] > 0.3 else 'no clear pattern'})")

def decade_traces(decade):
    g = growth[growth["decade"] == decade]
    traces = []
    for c in CONTINENTS:
        d = g[g["continent"] == c]
        traces.append(go.Scatter(
            x=d["gdp_pc_start"], y=d["growth"], mode="markers", name=c, legendgroup=c,
            text=d["country"], customdata=d[["pop_start"]],
            marker=dict(size=d["pop_start"], sizemode="area", sizeref=sizeref, sizemin=4,
                        color=COLORS[c], opacity=0.75, line=dict(width=0.6, color="white")),
            hovertemplate=("<b>%{text}</b><br>GDP per person at start: $%{x:,.0f}"
                           "<br>growth: %{y:.1f}% a year"
                           "<br>population: %{customdata[0]:,.0f} million<extra></extra>")))
    lx = np.log(g["gdp_pc_start"])
    b, a = np.polyfit(lx, g["growth"], 1)
    xs = np.exp(np.linspace(lx.min(), lx.max(), 50))
    traces.append(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=a + b * np.log(xs), mode="lines", hoverinfo="skip",
                             name="fitted line", line=dict(color="black", width=2, dash="dash")))
    # The decade's slope, drawn as a text trace so it moves with the animation
    # frames without touching the layout (layout changes reset the slider).
    traces.append(go.Scatter(x=[400], y=[12.6], mode="text", text=[label(decade)],
                             textposition="middle right", hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False,
                             textfont=dict(size=14)))
    return traces

fig = go.Figure(
    data=decade_traces(DECADES[0]),
    frames=[go.Frame(data=decade_traces(d), name=d) for d in DECADES],
)

steps = [dict(method="animate", label=d,
              args=[[d], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True),
                              transition=dict(duration=300))]) for d in DECADES]

fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="Starting income and growth over the following decade", x=0.01,
               y=0.985, yanchor="top", font=dict(size=15)),
    template="simple_white", height=640,
    xaxis=dict(type="log", title="GDP per person at start of decade (2021 PPP dollars, log scale)",
               range=[np.log10(350), np.log10(300000)], tickformat="$,.0f"),
    yaxis=dict(title="average annual growth, % per person", range=[-15, 14],
               zeroline=True, zerolinecolor="#bbbbbb"),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0, title=None,
                itemsizing="constant"),
    margin=dict(t=140, b=40, l=70, r=20),
    sliders=[dict(active=0, steps=steps, x=0.1, len=0.9, y=0, yanchor="top",
                  pad=dict(t=55, b=10),
                  currentvalue=dict(prefix="decade: ", visible=True, xanchor="left",
                                    font=dict(size=13)))],
    updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", showactive=False, direction="left",
                      x=0.1, xanchor="right", y=0, yanchor="top", pad=dict(t=65, r=10),
                      buttons=[dict(label="▶ play", method="animate",
                                    args=[None, dict(frame=dict(duration=1200, redraw=True),
                                                     transition=dict(duration=400),
                                                     fromcurrent=True)])])],
)
fig.show()
```

In the 1960s the line slopes *up*: the richest quarter of countries grew
`{python} f"{rich60:.1f}"` percent a year and the poorest quarter
`{python} f"{poor60:.1f}"`. The world was diverging. The 1980s and 1990s are flat. Then in
the 2000s the line tips clearly downward: the poorest quarter grew
`{python} f"{poor00:.1f}"` percent a year against `{python} f"{rich00:.1f}"` for the
richest. The 2010s keep the downward slope, though less steeply.

## Countries or people

Every country counts once in that fit, so Malawi weighs as much as India. Counting people
instead, by weighting each country by its population, tells a different story:

```{python}
#| label: fig-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Convergence slope by decade: how many percentage points of annual growth a country gained or lost for each log point (about 2.7 times) of higher starting income. Bars are 95 percent confidence intervals."

fig2 = go.Figure()
for col, se, name, color in [("slope", "se", "each country counts once", "#555555"),
                             ("slope_pop", "se_pop", "each person counts once", "#0072B2")]:
    fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=slopes["decade"], y=slopes[col], mode="lines+markers", name=name,
        line=dict(color=color, width=2.5), marker=dict(size=9),
        error_y=dict(type="data", array=1.96 * slopes[se], color=color, thickness=1.2),
        customdata=slopes[["countries"]],
        hovertemplate=(f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: slope %{{y:+.2f}}"
                       "<br>%{customdata[0]} countries<extra></extra>")))
fig2.add_hline(y=0, line_color="#999999", line_dash="dot")
fig2.add_annotation(x=0, y=1.6, xref="x", text="above zero: richer countries grew faster",
                    showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color="#888888", size=11))
fig2.add_annotation(x=0, y=-2.0, xref="x", text="below zero: poorer countries grew faster",
                    showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color="#888888", size=11))
fig2.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=400, yaxis_title="convergence slope",
                   yaxis_range=[-2.3, 1.9], legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0),
                   margin=dict(t=60))
fig2.show()
```

Weighted by people, convergence starts in the 1980s, twenty years earlier, with a slope of
`{python} f"{s.loc['1980s', 'slope_pop']:+.2f}"` against
`{python} f"{s.loc['1980s', 'slope']:+.2f}"` for countries. Go back to the first chart, set
it to the 1980s and hover over the two largest bubbles: China and India, among the poorest
countries in 1980, growing at 7 and 3 percent a year. Then click everything but Africa off
in the legend: `{python} f"{afr80_shrank}"` of Africa's `{python} f"{afr80_n}"` economies
shrank per person through that decade. Together
those two facts are the whole gap between the lines.

## What it means

Whether the world is converging depends on what you are asking. If the question is about
people, about how many of the world's poor live in economies that are catching up, the
answer has been yes since the 1980s, largely because of two countries. If the question is
whether a typical poor country can expect to catch up, the answer was no for forty years
and has been yes only since about 2000, a result Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian (2021)
find across several datasets. It is still young, and it was weaker in the 2010s than in the
2000s.

These are unconditional comparisons: they do not hold education, institutions or commodity
prices fixed, and the set of countries with data grows from
`{python} f"{s.loc['1960s', 'countries']}"` in the 1960s to
`{python} f"{s.loc['2010s', 'countries']}"` in the 2010s.

## Data and references

Feenstra, Robert C., Robert Inklaar, and Marcel P. Timmer. 2015. "The Next Generation of
the Penn World Table." *American Economic Review* 105 (10): 3150-3182. Data: PWT 11.0,
doi:10.34894/FABVLR, CC BY 4.0. Continents from Our World in Data.

Convergence." *Journal of Development Economics* 152: 102687.
